A relation $\mathcal{R}$ is in \cc{TF\Sigma_i^P} if the following conditions hold:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\mathcal{R}$ is total: for all $x \in \{ 0, 1\}^*$, there exists $y \in \{ 0, 1\}^*$ such that $(x, y) \in \mathcal{R}$.
        \item $\mathcal{R}$ is polynomial: For all $(x, y) \in \mathcal{R}$, $|y| \leq \poly(|x|)$.
        \item There exists a polynomial time Turing machine $M$ and polynomials $p_1(n), \dots, p_{i-1}(n)$ such that 
        \[(x, y) \in R \iff \forall z_1 \in \{ 0, 1\}^{p_1(|x|)} \exists z_2 \in \{ 0, 1\}^{p_2(|x|)} \forall z_3 \in \{ 0, 1\}^{p_3(|x|)} \dots V(x, y, z_1, \dots, z_{i-1})\text{ accepts.}\]
    \end{enumerate}
statement_text: A relation R is in TFΣ_i^P if the following conditions hold: R is total: for all x ∈ { 0, 1}^* , there exists y ∈ { 0, 1}^* such that (x, y) ∈ R . R is polynomial: For all (x, y) ∈ R , |y| ≤ poly (|x|) . There exists a polynomial time Turing machine M and polynomials p_1(n), ... , p_ i-1 (n) such that \[(x, y) ∈ R ⟺ ∀ z_1 ∈ { 0, 1}^ p_1(|x|) ∃ z_2 ∈ { 0, 1}^ p_2(|x|) ∀ z_3 ∈ { 0, 1}^ p_3(|x|) ... V(x, y, z_1, ... , z_ i-1 ) accepts. \]

paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_tex: A relation $\mathcal{R}$ is in \cc{TFU\Sigma_i^P} if it is in \cc{TF\Sigma_i^P} and for all $x \in \{ 0, 1\}^*$, there exists exactly one $y$ such that $(x, y) \in \mathcal{R}$.
statement_text: A relation R is in TFUΣ_i^P if it is in TFΣ_i^P and for all x ∈ { 0, 1}^* , there exists exactly one y such that (x, y) ∈ R .

label: def: reduction
paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_text: Let R , Q be two search problems. A many-to-one reduction from R to Q is defined as two polynomial time computable functions f, g such that for all x ∈ π_1( R ), y ∈ { 0, 1}^* , the following holds. \[ (x, g(y)) ∈ R impliedby (f(x), y) ∈ Q \]

label: def:relation_total
paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_tex:
\label{def:relation_total}
    Let $\mathcal{R}$ be a relation and let $A = \{ (x, \bot) : x \notin \pi_1(\mathcal{R})\}$. We define the completion of $\mathcal{R}$ as $\overline{\mathcal{R}} := \mathcal{R} \cup A$.
statement_text: Let R be a relation and let A = { (x, bot ) : x ∉ π_1( R )} . We define the completion of R as overline R := R ∪ A .

paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_tex: We say $\mathcal{R}$ has a polynomial time algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ if $\mathcal{A}$ runs in polynomial time for all inputs in $\{ 0, 1\}^*$ and for all $x \in \pi_1(\mathcal{R})$, $(x, \mathcal{A}(x)) \in \mathcal{R}$.
statement_text: We say R has a polynomial time algorithm A if A runs in polynomial time for all inputs in { 0, 1}^* and for all x ∈ π_1( R ) , (x, A (x)) ∈ R .

paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_tex: Let $\mathcal{Q}$ be a total search problem. We say $\mathcal{R}$ has a polynomial time algorithm $\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}$ if $\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}$ runs in polynomial time and for all $x \in \pi_1(\mathcal{R})$ and all instantiations of the oracle $\mathcal{Q}$, $(x, \mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}(x)) \in \mathcal{R}$.
statement_text: Let Q be a total search problem. We say R has a polynomial time algorithm A ^ Q if A ^ Q runs in polynomial time and for all x ∈ π_1( R ) and all instantiations of the oracle Q , (x, A ^ Q (x)) ∈ R .

paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_tex: \cc{PLS} is defined as all problems which are many-to-one reducible to \prob{Sink-of-DAG}, which is defined as follows. Given $\poly(n)$ size circuits $S: [2^n] \rightarrow [2^n]$ (successor circuit) and $V: [2^n] \rightarrow [2^n]$ (value circuit), find $v$ such that $S(v) \neq v$ and either $S(S(v)) = S(v)$ or $V(S(v)) \leq V(v)$.
statement_text: PLS is defined as all problems which are many-to-one reducible to sc Sink-of-DAG , which is defined as follows. Given poly (n) size circuits S: [2^n] → [2^n] (successor circuit) and V: [2^n] → [2^n] (value circuit), find v such that S(v) ≠ v and either S(S(v)) = S(v) or V(S(v)) ≤ V(v) .
title: PLS and sc Sink-of-DAG

paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_tex:
Given a successor circuit $S : \{0, 1\}^n \to \{0, 1\}^n$,  a source $s \in \{0, 1\}^n$, a target index $T \in [2^n]$, and a verifier circuit 
$W : \{0, 1\}^n \times [T] \to \{0, 1\}$ with the guarantee that for $(x, i) \in \{0, 1\}^n \times [T]$, $W(x, i) = 1$ if and only if $x = S^{i-1}(s)$, find the string $v \in \{0, 1\}^n$ such that $W(v, T) = 1$.
statement_text: Given a successor circuit S : {0, 1}^n → {0, 1}^n , a source s ∈ {0, 1}^n , a target index T ∈ [2^n] , and a verifier circuit W : {0, 1}^n × [T] → {0, 1} with the guarantee that for (x, i) ∈ {0, 1}^n × [T] , W(x, i) = 1 if and only if x = S^ i-1 (s) , find the string v ∈ {0, 1}^n such that W(v, T) = 1 .
title: sc Sink-of-Verifiable-Line

paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_tex:
\prob{Unique-End-of-Potential-Line} is defined as follows. Given two $\poly(n)$ size circuits $S, P : \bit^n \rightarrow \bit^n$, such that $P(0^n) = 0^n \neq S(0^n)$, and a value circuit $V:\bit^n \rightarrow \{0, 1, \hdots, 2^{m-1}\}$ where $V(0^n) = 0$. Find one of the following:
\begin{itemize}
    \item A point $x \in \bit^n$ such that $P(S(x)) \neq x$.

    \item A point $x \in \bit^n$ such that $x \neq S(x), P(S(X)) = x$ and $V(S(x)) - V(x) \leq 0$.

    \item A point $x \in \bit^n$ such that $S(P(x)) \neq x \neq 0^n$. 

    \item Two points $x, y \in \bit^n$, such that $x \neq y$, $x \neq S(x)$, $y \neq S(y)$, and either $V(x) = V(y)$ or $V(x) < V(y) < S(x)$.
\end{itemize}
\cc{UEOPL} is defined as all problems which are many-to-one reducible to \prob{Unique-End-of-Potential-Line}.
statement_text: sc Unique-End-of-Potential-Line is defined as follows. Given two poly (n) size circuits S, P : { 0, 1 }^n → { 0, 1 }^n , such that P(0^n) = 0^n ≠ S(0^n) , and a value circuit V:{ 0, 1 }^n → {0, 1, hdots , 2^ m-1 } where V(0^n) = 0 . Find one of the following: A point x ∈ { 0, 1 }^n such that P(S(x)) ≠ x . A point x ∈ { 0, 1 }^n such that x ≠ S(x), P(S(X)) = x and V(S(x)) - V(x) ≤ 0 . A point x ∈ { 0, 1 }^n such that S(P(x)) ≠ x ≠ 0^n . Two points x, y ∈ { 0, 1 }^n , such that x ≠ y , x ≠ S(x) , y ≠ S(y) , and either V(x) = V(y) or V(x) < V(y) < S(x) . UEOPL is defined as all problems which are many-to-one reducible to sc Unique-End-of-Potential-Line .
title: sc Unique-End-of-Potential-Line

paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_tex:
\label{lem: sovl_to_ueopl}

statement_text: sc Sink-of-Verifiable-Line reduces to sc Unique-End-of-Potential-Line under relativizing reductions.

statement_text: We say that a search problem R ⊆ { 0, 1}^* × { 0, 1}^* is in the class PromiseFΣ_i^P if it satisfies the following conditions. For all x ∈ π_1( R ) , and for all y s.t. (x, y) ∈ R , |y| ≤ poly (|x|) . There exists a polynomial time verifier V and polynomials p_1(n), ... , p_ i-1 (n) such that the following holds: for all x ∈ π_1(R) , \[(x, y) ∈ R ⟺ ∀ z_1 ∈ { 0, 1}^ p_1(|x|) ∃ z_2 ∈ { 0, 1}^ p_2(|x|) ∀ z_3 ∈ { 0, 1}^ p_3(|x|) ... V(x, y, z_1, ... , z_ i-1 ) accepts. \]

label: def: mu-dsr
paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_tex:
\label{def: mu-dsr}
    Let $\mu:\bit^* \rightarrow \N$ be a function. A \cc{PromiseF\Sigma_i^P} problem $\mathcal{R}$ is (randomized) $\cc{\Sigma_{i-1}^P}$-$\mu$-downward-self-reducible ($\mu$-d.s.r.) if there is a (randomized) polynomial-time oracle algorithm $\mathcal{A}^{\cc{\Sigma_{i-1}^P}, \overline{\mathcal{R}}}$ for $\mathcal{R}$ that on input $x \in \pi_1(\mathcal{R})$, makes queries to a $\mathcal{R}$-oracle on instances $y$ such that $y$ satisfies the promise of $\mathcal{R}$, $|y| \leq |x| + \poly(\mu(x))$, and $\mu(y) < \mu(x)$. We simply say that such a problem is $\mu$-downward-self-reducible when $\cc{\Sigma_{i-1}^P}$ is clear from context.
statement_text: Let μ:{ 0, 1 }^* → N be a function. A PromiseFΣ_i^P problem R is (randomized) Σ_ i-1 ^P - μ -downward-self-reducible ( μ -d.s.r.) if there is a (randomized) polynomial-time oracle algorithm A ^ Σ_ i-1 ^P , overline R for R that on input x ∈ π_1( R ) , makes queries to a R -oracle on instances y such that y satisfies the promise of R , |y| ≤ |x| + poly (μ(x)) , and μ(y) < μ(x) . We simply say that such a problem is μ -downward-self-reducible when Σ_ i-1 ^P is clear from context.

label: thm:mu-dsr
paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_tex:
\label{thm:mu-dsr}
    Let $\mathcal{R}$ be a search problem in \cc{PromiseF\Sigma_i^P} which has a (randomized) $\mu$-d.s.r. If $\mu(x) \leq p(|x|)$ for a polynomial $p$, then there is a (randomized) reduction from $\mathcal{R}$ to $\PLS^{\cc{\Sigma_{i-1}^P}}$. Furthermore, if $\mathcal{R}$ has unique solutions, then there is a (randomized) reduction from $\mathcal{R}$ to $\cc{UEOPL}^{\cc{\Sigma_{i-1}^P}}$.
statement_text: Let R be a search problem in PromiseFΣ_i^P which has a (randomized) μ -d.s.r. If μ(x) ≤ p(|x|) for a polynomial p , then there is a (randomized) reduction from R to PLS ^ Σ_ i-1 ^P . Furthermore, if R has unique solutions, then there is a (randomized) reduction from R to UEOPL ^ Σ_ i-1 ^P .

label: cor: promise_fsat
paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_tex:
\label{cor: promise_fsat}
    If \prob{PromiseFSAT} is $\mu$-d.s.r for polynomially bounded $\mu$, then \prob{SAT} reduces to \cc{PLS}. If \prob{Promise-Unique-FSAT} is $\mu$-d.s.r for polynomially bounded $\mu$, then \prob{SAT} reduces to \cc{UEOPL}.
statement_text: If sc PromiseFSAT is μ -d.s.r for polynomially bounded μ , then sc SAT reduces to PLS . If sc Promise-Unique-FSAT is μ -d.s.r for polynomially bounded μ , then sc SAT reduces to UEOPL .

label: cor: mu-d.s.r
paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_tex:
\label{cor: mu-d.s.r}
    Let $\mu:\bit^* \rightarrow \N$ be a function bounded by some polynomial. Any \cc{TF\Sigma_i^P} problem which is $\mu$-d.s.r with a \cc{\Sigma_{i-1}^P} oracle is in \cc{PLS^{\Sigma_{i-1}^P}}. Any \cc{TFU\Sigma_i^P} problem which is $\mu$-d.s.r with a \cc{\Sigma_{i-1}^P} oracle is in \cc{UEOPL^{\Sigma_{i-1}^P}}.
statement_text: Let μ:{ 0, 1 }^* → N be a function bounded by some polynomial. Any TFΣ_i^P problem which is μ -d.s.r with a Σ_ i-1 ^P oracle is in PLS^ Σ_ i-1 ^P . Any TFUΣ_i^P problem which is μ -d.s.r with a Σ_ i-1 ^P oracle is in UEOPL^ Σ_ i-1 ^P .

statement_tex: The problem \prob{Empty} is defined as follows. Given a $\poly(n)$ size circuit $C: [2^n - 1] \rightarrow [2^n]$, output $y$ such that $y \notin \text{range$(C)$}$.

label: def: essentially_unique
paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_text: We say that a total search problem R ∈ TFΣ_i^P ( i ≥ 2 ) has essentially unique solutions if there exist two verifiers V_1, V_2 such that the following hold. V_1 is testable in polynomial time with an Σ_ i-2 ^P oracle and V_2 is testable in polynomial time with an Σ_ i-1 ^P oracle. For all x , either there exists a y such that V_1(x, y) = 1 and (x, y) ∈ R , or else there exists a unique y such that V_2(x, y) = 1 and (x, y) ∈ R .
title: Essentially Unique Solutions

paper_title: Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy
statement_text: For any relation R with essentially unique solutions and verifiers V_1, V_2 , we define R _u as follows. For any x ∈ π_1( R ) such that there exists y where V_1(x, y) = 1 , (x, y) ∈ R _u if and only if y is the lexicographically smallest y where V_1(x,y) = 1 . For any x ∈ π_1( R ) such that V_1(x, y) = 0 for all y , (x, y) ∈ R _u if and only if (x, y) ∈ R .

Let $k \geq 3$. A $k$-ary operation $\varphi: A^k \to A$ on a finite set $A$ is called \emph{generalized majority-minority} (GMM) if, for all $a,b \in A$,
\begin{gather*}
    \varphi(x, y, \ldots, y) = \varphi(y, x, \ldots, y) = \ldots = \varphi(y, y, \ldots, x) = y \quad \text{for all } x, y \in \{a, b\}, \\
    \text{or} \\
    \varphi(x, y, \ldots, y) = \varphi(y, y, \ldots, x) = x \quad \text{for all } x, y \in \{a, b\}.
\end{gather*}
In the first case, we say that $a, b\in A$ is a \emph{majority pair} for $\varphi$, and in the second case $a, b\in A$ is a \emph{minority pair}.
statement_text: Let k ≥ 3 . A k -ary operation φ: A^k → A on a finite set A is called generalized majority-minority (GMM) if, for all a,b ∈ A , φ(x, y, ... , y) = φ(y, x, ... , y) = ... = φ(y, y, ... , x) = y quad for all x, y ∈ {a, b}, or φ(x, y, ... , y) = φ(y, y, ... , x) = x quad for all x, y ∈ {a, b}. statement_tex:
[CSP as a homomorphism problem \cite{BULATOV200531}] $\,$
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a relational structure over a vocabulary $R_1, \ldots, R_n$. In the \emph{constraint satisfaction problem} associated with $\mathcal{A}$, denoted by CSP($\mathcal{A}$), the question is: given a structure $\mathcal{X}$ over the same vocabulary, does there exist a homomorphism from $\mathcal{X}$ to $\mathcal{A}$? If the answer is positive, we call the instance $\mathcal{X}$ \emph{satisfiable}; otherwise, it is \emph{unsatisfiable}. We refer to $\mathcal{A}$ as the \emph{target structure} and to $\mathcal{X}$ as the \emph{instance (or input) structure}.

If the answer is positive, we call the instance X satisfiable ; otherwise, it is unsatisfiable . We refer to A as the target structure and to X as the instance (or input) structure .

statement_tex:
An instance of the $3$-LIN($p$) problem is a system of linear equations $A \cdot \bm{x} = \bm{b}$ over the field $\mathbb{Z}_p$, where each equation involves exactly three variables. If $R$ is the solution space of $A \cdot \bm{x} = \bm{b}$, then the operation $\mu(x, y, z) = x - y + z$ is a polymorphism of $R$. Indeed, suppose that $\bm{x}, \bm{y}, \bm{z} \in R$, then
$$
A \cdot \mu(\bm{x}, \bm{y}, \bm{z}) = A \cdot (\bm{x} - \bm{y} + \bm{z}) = A \cdot \bm{x} - A \cdot \bm{y} + A \cdot \bm{z} = \bm{b} - \bm{b} + \bm{b} = \bm{b}.
$$
statement_text: An instance of the 3 -LIN( p ) problem is a system of linear equations A · bm x = bm b over the field Z _p , where each equation involves exactly three variables. If R is the solution space of A · bm x = bm b , then the operation μ(x, y, z) = x - y + z is a polymorphism of R . Indeed, suppose that bm x , bm y , bm z ∈ R , then A · μ(bm x , bm y , bm z ) = A · (bm x - bm y + bm z ) = A · bm x - A · bm y + A · bm z = bm b - bm b + bm b = bm b .

UU^{-1}U = gH(gH)^{-1}gH = gH H g^{-1} gH = g H H H = gH = U.

statement_tex:
If $F$ is a Frege proof system, an extended Frege proof is a sequence of formulas $\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_k$ such that each $\theta_i$ is either derived from some earlier $\theta_j$'s by a rule from $F$, or has the form $q \equiv \psi$, where:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item the atom $q$ appears in neither $\psi$ nor in any $\theta_j$ for $j < i$,
    \item the atom $q$ does not appear in $\theta_k$,
    \item $\alpha \equiv \beta$ abbreviates $(\alpha \wedge \beta) \vee (\neg \alpha \wedge \neg \beta)$.
\end{enumerate}
A formula of this form is called an \emph{extension axiom}, and $q$ is called an \emph{extension atom}. An \emph{extended Frege proof system} $EF$ is a proof system in which proofs are extended Frege proofs.
statement_text: If F is a Frege proof system, an extended Frege proof is a sequence of formulas θ_1, ... , θ_k such that each θ_i is either derived from some earlier θ_j 's by a rule from F , or has the form q equiv ψ , where: the atom q appears in neither ψ nor in any θ_j for j < i , the atom q does not appear in θ_k , α equiv β abbreviates (α wedge β) vee ( ¬ α wedge ¬ β) . A formula of this form is called an extension axiom , and q is called an extension atom . An extended Frege proof system EF is a proof system in which proofs are extended Frege proofs.

label: thm: Cubical Complex
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_text: Let F be a 3-SAT formula with n variables. The set of satisfying assignments S ⊆ {0,1}^n forms a cubical complex C(F) , where: Vertices correspond to satisfying assignments. k -faces correspond to k -dimensional subcubes where all 2^k assignments satisfy F . Topological queries about C(F) (e.g., connectedness, Betti numbers) reduce to 3-SAT instances.

label: thm:unstructured
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_text: Let F be a random 3-SAT instance at clause density α>4.26 . Then with probability 1-o(1) : Its solution space S(F) decomposes into 2^ Ω(n) disconnected clusters. The cubical complex of S(F) has exponentially large Betti numbers (e.g.\ β_2(S(F))=2^ Ω(n) ). The primal constraint graph of F has treewidth Ω(n) . In particular, S(F) admits no global ordering or low-dimensional traversal.

label: lem:sat-4sat-to-3sat
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_tex:
\label{lem:sat-4sat-to-3sat}

Let $L = SAT{}$ and suppose $R:L\to\threesat{}$ is a polynomial-time satisfiability-preserving reduction that is \emph{cubical} and \emph{homologically faithful} (discussion on this is delayed to Section 5.2 Conditions 1 and 2). If $F \in L$ has a solution-space cubical complex $S(F)$ with $\beta_{2}(S(F))\geq f(n)$ for some $f(n)=\omega(poly(n))$, then the reduced instance $F^{\prime}=R(F)$ satisfies
\[
\beta_{2}\big(S(F^{\prime})\big)\ \geq\ \beta_{2}\big(S(F)\big)\ =\ \Omega(f(n)).
\]
In particular, the reduction from SAT to 3-SAT does not collapse exponential second Betti numbers.

If F ∈ L has a solution-space cubical complex S(F) with β_ 2 (S(F)) ≥ f(n) for some f(n)=ω(poly(n)) , then the reduced instance F^ prime =R(F) satisfies \[ β_ 2 (S(F^ prime ) )\ ≥ \ β_ 2 (S(F) )\ =\ Ω(f(n)). \] In particular, the reduction from SAT to 3-SAT does not collapse exponential second Betti numbers.

faithfulness
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_tex:
\label{lem:Homological 
faithfulness}

  Let $C$ be any CNF formula on variables $x_1,\dots,x_N$, and let
$C'$ be the 3-CNF formula obtained from $C$ by the standard clause-splitting
reduction: every clause $\ell_1\vee\ell_2\vee\cdots\vee\ell_m$ with $m\ge 4$
is replaced by the chain of 3-clauses
\[
(\ell_1\vee\ell_2\vee a_1)\wedge(\neg a_1\vee\ell_3\vee a_2)\wedge\cdots
\wedge(\neg a_{k-1}\vee\ell_{k+1}\vee a_k)\wedge(\neg a_k\vee\ell_{m-1}\vee\ell_m),
\]
where $k=m-3$ and $a_1,\dots,a_k$ are fresh auxiliary variables.

Then the inclusion of cubical solution complexes
\[
\Sol(C)\;\hookrightarrow\;\Sol(C')
\]
is a homotopy equivalence. In particular, for every field $\Bbb F$ and every $k\ge0$ the induced map on homology
\[
H_k\bigl(\Sol(C);\Bbb F\bigr)\;\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\;H_k\bigl(\Sol(C');\Bbb F\bigr)
\]
is an isomorphism.

label: thm:betti-monotonicity
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_tex:
\label{thm:betti-monotonicity}
Let \(R\) be a cubical, homologically faithful reduction. Then, for every \(k\),
\[
\beta_k\bigl(S(x)\bigr) \le \beta_k\bigl(S(R(x))\bigr).
\]
In particular, if \(\beta_k(S(x)) = 2^{\Omega(N)}\) then \(\beta_k(S(R(x))) = 2^{\Omega(N)}\).
statement_text: Let \(R\) be a cubical, homologically faithful reduction. Then, for every \(k\), \[ β_k l(S(x) r) ≤ β_k l(S(R(x)) r). \] In particular, if \(β_k(S(x)) = 2^ Ω(N) \) then \(β_k(S(R(x))) = 2^ Ω(N) \).
title: Betti Monotonicity under Faithful Embeddings

\label{lem:homology-injectivity}

\]

label: thm:non-embedding-hardness
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_text: Computing \(β_k(K)\) for \(k ≥ 2\) on a cubical complex \(K ⊆ {0,1}^N\) is \(\# P \)-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions. In particular, unless \(\# P ⊆ FP \), no algorithm in the standard Boolean decision-tree or subcube-query model can compute \(β_k(K)\) in worst-case time \(2^ o(N) \).
title: Topology-Destroying Reductions are Hard

statement_tex:
Under the assumption \(\PH\not\supseteq\#\Pclass\), no polynomial-time (even randomized) algorithm can:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Compute \(\beta_k(S(F))\) exactly for arbitrary 3-SAT \(F\).
  \item Approximate \(\beta_k(S(F))\) within any \(2^{o(N)}\) factor.
  \item Distinguish \(\beta_k(S(F))=0\) from \(\beta_k(S(F))\ge2^{cN}\) with non-negligible advantage.
\end{itemize}
Hence any property of the form
\(\mathcal P_N(F)\equiv[\beta_2(S(F))\ge2^{cN}]\)
fails the “constructivity” requirement of Razborov–Rudich’s Natural Proofs framework, despite meeting largeness and usefulness.

Approximate \(β_k(S(F))\) within any \(2^ o(N) \) factor. Distinguish \(β_k(S(F))=0\) from \(β_k(S(F)) ≥ 2^ cN \) with non-negligible advantage. Hence any property of the form \(P_N(F)equiv [β_2(S(F)) ≥ 2^ cN ]\) fails the “constructivity” requirement of Razborov–Rudich’s Natural Proofs framework, despite meeting largeness and usefulness.

label: thm:Proxies
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_tex:
\label{thm:Proxies}
Fix a constant radius $r\ge 1$ and let $q(\cdot)$ be any polynomial. 
There exist two families of 3-CNF formulas
\[
\{F^{\mathrm{easy}}_{n}\}_{n\ge 1},\qquad \{F^{\mathrm{hard}}_{n}\}_{n\ge 1},
\]
and a function $m_n\to\infty$ (which may be chosen as $m_n=2^{c n}$ for some $c>0$) with the following properties for every $n$:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[\textup{(i)}] The final number of Boolean variables satisfies $N_n=\Theta(m_n)$ for both families (each gadget is constant-size).
  \item[\textup{(ii)}] The incidence graphs of both families have treewidth $O(1)$.
  \item[\textup{(iii)}] \textbf{Local-indistinguishability:} For any choice of at most $q(n)$ vertex-centered radius-$r$ neighborhoods, the induced labeled subgraphs of $F^{\mathrm{easy}}_{n}$ and $F^{\mathrm{hard}}_{n}$ are identical on all those neighborhoods. Hence any proxy that inspects at most $q(n)$ radius-$r$ views cannot distinguish the two families on input size~$n$.
  \item[\textup{(iv)}] \textbf{Topological gap:} $\displaystyle \beta_2\bigl(S(F^{\mathrm{hard}}_{n})\bigr)\ge m_n$ while $\beta_2\bigl(S(F^{\mathrm{easy}}_{n})\bigr)=O(1)$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, choosing $m_n=2^{c n}$ yields an exponential gap in $\beta_2$ that local proxies of radius $r$ and $q(n)$ inspections fail to detect. Expressed in terms of the final variable count $N_n=\Theta(m_n)$, one obtains $\beta_2\bigl(S(F^{\mathrm{hard}}_{n})\bigr)\ge 2^{c' N_n}$ for some constant $c'>0$.
statement_text: Fix a constant radius r ≥ 1 and let q( · ) be any polynomial. There exist two families of 3-CNF formulas \[ {F^ easy _ n }_ n ≥ 1 ,qquad {F^ hard _ n }_ n ≥ 1 , \] and a function m_n → ∞ (which may be chosen as m_n=2^ c n for some c>0 ) with the following properties for every n : The final number of Boolean variables satisfies N_n=Θ(m_n) for both families (each gadget is constant-size). The incidence graphs of both families have treewidth O(1) . bf Local-indistinguishability: For any choice of at most q(n) vertex-centered radius- r neighborhoods, the induced labeled subgraphs of F^ easy _ n and F^ hard _ n are identical on all those neighborhoods. Hence any proxy that inspects at most q(n) radius- r views cannot distinguish the two families on input size n . bf Topological gap: β_2 l(S(F^ hard _ n ) r) ≥ m_n while β_2 l(S(F^ easy _ n ) r)=O(1) . In particular, choosing m_n=2^ c n yields an exponential gap in β_2 that local proxies of radius r and q(n) inspections fail to detect. Expressed in terms of the final variable count N_n=Θ(m_n) , one obtains β_2 l(S(F^ hard _ n ) r) ≥ 2^ c' N_n for some constant c'>0 .

label: thm:hamiltonian-gap-formal
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_tex:
\label{thm:hamiltonian-gap-formal}
Let $F$ be a 3-SAT formula on $n$ variables and let $S(F)\subset\{0,1\}^n$ be its solution
set.  Suppose there exist constants $c',c>0$ such that
\[
\beta_2\bigl(S(F)\bigr)\;\ge\; 2^{c' n}.
\]
Let $H_F$ be a physically $k$-local Hamiltonian acting on $n$ qubits satisfying the
following assumptions.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[(A1)] (Ground-space encoding) The ground-space of $H_F$ is exactly the linear span
    of computational-basis states corresponding to satisfying assignments:
    \[
      \mathcal{G} := \Span\{\ket{x} : x\in S(F)\},
    \]
    and $H_F\ket{\psi}=0$ for all $\ket{\psi}\in\mathcal G$.
  \item[(A2)] (Cubical-preserving drivers / exponential inter-cluster suppression)
    Partition $S(F)=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^K C_i$ into clusters (connected components under
    single-bit flips) so that $K\ge 2^{c'n}$.  There exists $c_1>0$ and a (fixed)
    polynomial $p(n)$ with the following property: for every pair of distinct clusters
    $C_i\neq C_j$ and every pair of basis states $x\in C_i$, $y\in C_j$,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:offdiag-bound}
      \bigl|\langle x \,|\, H_F \,|\, y\rangle\bigr| \;\le\; p(n)\,e^{-c_1 n}.
    \end{equation}
    (Intuitively: all local drivers induce exponentially small matrix elements between
    different clusters.)
  \item[(A3)] (Polynomial locality degree) For every basis state $\ket{x}$ the number of
    basis states $\ket{y}$ with $\langle x|H_F|y\rangle\neq 0$ is at most $q(n)$ for some
    fixed polynomial $q$.  This holds for any $k$-local Hamiltonian with $k=O(1)$.
\end{enumerate}
Then there exists $a>0$ (depending only on $c_1,c',p,q$) such that the spectral gap
above the ground-space satisfies
\[
  g(H_F) \;\le\; 2\,e^{-a n}.
\]
In particular the gap is at most exponentially small in $n$.

Suppose there exist constants c',c>0 such that \[ β_2 l(S(F) r) ≥ 2^ c' n . \] Let H_F be a physically k -local Hamiltonian acting on n qubits satisfying the following assumptions. (Ground-space encoding) The ground-space of H_F is exactly the linear span of computational-basis states corresponding to satisfying assignments: \[ G := Span {ket x : x ∈ S(F)}, \] and H_Fket ψ =0 for all ket ψ ∈ G . (Cubical-preserving drivers / exponential inter-cluster suppression) Partition S(F)= sqcup_ i=1 ^K C_i into clusters (connected components under single-bit flips) so that K ≥ 2^ c'n . There exists c_1>0 and a (fixed) polynomial p(n) with the following property: for every pair of distinct clusters C_i ≠ C_j and every pair of basis states x ∈ C_i , y ∈ C_j , l|le x | H_F | yrangle r| ≤ p(n) e^ -c_1 n . (Intuitively: all local drivers induce exponentially small matrix elements between different clusters.) (Polynomial locality degree) For every basis state ket x the number of basis states ket y with le x|H_F|yrangle ≠ 0 is at most q(n) for some fixed polynomial q . This holds for any k -local Hamiltonian with k=O(1) . Then there exists a>0 (depending only on c_1,c',p,q ) such that the spectral gap above the ground-space satisfies \[ g(H_F) ≤ 2 e^ -a n . \] In particular the gap is at most exponentially small in n .
title: Hamiltonian spectral-gap hardness

statement_tex:

label: lem:homology-preservation
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_tex:
\label{lem:homology-preservation}
Let $K$ be a cubical complex obtained from a CNF instance (or its solution complex) that contains subcomplexes
\[
  C_1,\dots,C_M \subseteq K
\]
(each $C_i$ supported on a small set of variables/clauses, a ``gadget''), and suppose the $C_i$ are pairwise disjoint as subcomplexes of $K$ (or can be made disjoint by the variable-duplication / padding procedure described in later in this Appendix). Let $K'$ be the complex obtained from $K$ by (i) duplicating variable/clauses as needed so that gadget supports become vertex-disjoint, and (ii) adding a linking subcomplex
\[
  L = \bigcup_{\ell} L_\ell
\]
(consisting of equality clauses / small wiring gadgets and any expander edges used in the amplification) which attaches to the gadgets in a local, controlled way.

Assume the following ``locality and acyclicity'' conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[(A1)] Each linking component $L_\ell$ is contractible (that is, $H_j(L_\ell)=0$ for all $j\ge 1$).
  \item[(A2)] For every $i$ and every linking component $L_\ell$ we have that the intersection $C_i\cap L_\ell$ is either empty or contractible (in particular $H_j(C_i\cap L_\ell)=0$ for all $j\ge 1$).
  \item[(A3)] No $(k+1)$-cell of $K'$ has support that intersects more than one distinct gadget $C_i$ (equivalently, every $(k+1)$-cell is incident to cells lying in at most one gadget-support $C_i$).
\end{enumerate}
Then for every homological degree $k\ge 0$ the inclusion $i: \bigsqcup_{i=1}^M C_i \hookrightarrow K'$ induces an injection on $H_k$, and in particular
\[
  \beta_k(K') \;\ge\; \sum_{i=1}^M \beta_k(C_i).
\]
If, moreover, the gadget cycles $\{\,[\gamma_i]\,\}$ were independent in $H_k(K)$ (so $\beta_k(K)=\sum_i\beta_k(C_i)$), then duplication/wiring preserves independence and
\[
  \beta_k(K') = \beta_k(K) = \sum_{i=1}^M \beta_k(C_i).
\]

Let K' be the complex obtained from K by (i) duplicating variable/clauses as needed so that gadget supports become vertex-disjoint, and (ii) adding a linking subcomplex \[ L = cup_ ell L_ell \] (consisting of equality clauses / small wiring gadgets and any expander edges used in the amplification) which attaches to the gadgets in a local, controlled way. Assume the following ``locality and acyclicity'' conditions hold: Each linking component L_ell is contractible (that is, H_j(L_ell )=0 for all j ≥ 1 ). For every i and every linking component L_ell we have that the intersection C_i ∩ L_ell is either empty or contractible (in particular H_j(C_i ∩ L_ell )=0 for all j ≥ 1 ). No (k+1) -cell of K' has support that intersects more than one distinct gadget C_i (equivalently, every (k+1) -cell is incident to cells lying in at most one gadget-support C_i ). Then for every homological degree k ≥ 0 the inclusion i: sqcup_ i=1 ^M C_i hookrightarrow K' induces an injection on H_k , and in particular \[ β_k(K') ≥ Σ _ i=1 ^M β_k(C_i). \] If, moreover, the gadget cycles { [γ_i] } were independent in H_k(K) (so β_k(K)= Σ _iβ_k(C_i) ), then duplication/wiring preserves independence and \[ β_k(K') = β_k(K) = Σ _ i=1 ^M β_k(C_i). \]

label: lem:param-mapping
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_tex:
\label{lem:param-mapping}
Let the base-graph parameter be $n_0$. Suppose the construction uses $G=C\,n_0$ gadgets and the base-encoding produces $n_{\mathrm{base}}=D\,n_0$ variables. Let the average number of auxiliary (gadget-local) variables per gadget be $k_g$ (possibly depending on $n_0$). Then the final number of variables is
\[
N \;=\; n_{\mathrm{base}} + k_g\cdot G \;=\; (D + C k_g)\, n_0.
\]
Consequently, an intermediate bound of the form $\beta_2 = 2^{c n_0}$ can be rewritten in terms of $N$ as
\[
\beta_2 \;=\; 2^{c' N},\qquad c'=\frac{c}{D + C k_g}.
\]
In particular:
\begin{itemize}
  \item If $k_g=O(1)$ then $c'=\Theta(c)$ and exponential-in-$n_0$ implies exponential-in-$N$ (constant factor loss in exponent).
  \item If $k_g=\Theta(\log n_0)$ and $G=\Theta(n_0)$ then $N=\Theta(n_0\log n_0)$ and a linear-in-$n_0$ Betti (e.g.\ $\beta_2=\Theta(n_0)$) becomes $\beta_2=\Theta\!\big(N/\log N\big)$.
\end{itemize}
statement_text: Let the base-graph parameter be n_0 . Suppose the construction uses G=C n_0 gadgets and the base-encoding produces n_ base =D n_0 variables. Let the average number of auxiliary (gadget-local) variables per gadget be k_g (possibly depending on n_0 ). Then the final number of variables is \[ N = n_ base + k_g · G = (D + C k_g) n_0. \] Consequently, an intermediate bound of the form β_2 = 2^ c n_0 can be rewritten in terms of N as \[ β_2 = 2^ c' N ,qquad c'=frac c D + C k_g . \] In particular: If k_g=O(1) then c'=Θ(c) and exponential-in- n_0 implies exponential-in- N (constant factor loss in exponent). If k_g=Θ( log n_0) and G=Θ(n_0) then N=Θ(n_0 log n_0) and a linear-in- n_0 Betti (e.g.\ β_2=Θ(n_0) ) becomes β_2=Θ (N/ log N ) .
title: Parameter mapping and exponent degradation

label: lem:no-cross-filling-ownership
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_tex:
\label{lem:no-cross-filling-ownership}
Assume the gadget construction of Appendix~B with the following ownership condition:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Ownership:} each base variable $x_{v,c}$ is referenced by equality/consistency clauses for at most one gadget (i.e.\ at most one gadget enforces $x_{v,c}\leftrightarrow x_{v,c}^{(i)}$).
\end{quote}

Then for distinct gadgets $i\neq j$ there exists no 3-chain $\beta$ with
\[
\partial_3\beta \;=\; a_i\gamma_i + a_j\gamma_j
\qquad\text{with }a_i,a_j\neq 0,
\]
where $\gamma_i,\gamma_j$ are the gadget-local 2-cycles witnessing independent homology classes.
statement_text: Assume the gadget construction of Appendix B with the following ownership condition: Ownership: each base variable x_ v,c is referenced by equality/consistency clauses for at most one gadget (i.e.\ at most one gadget enforces x_ v,c ↔ x_ v,c ^ (i) ). Then for distinct gadgets i ≠ j there exists no 3-chain β with \[ partial _3β = a_iγ_i + a_jγ_j qquad with a_i,a_j ≠ 0, \] where γ_i,γ_j are the gadget-local 2-cycles witnessing independent homology classes.
title: No cross-gadget filling under ownership

label: lem:ownership-exists
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_tex:
\label{lem:ownership-exists}
One may assign to every base literal $x_{v,c}$ an arbitrary owning gadget (if any gadget references it); for non-owner gadgets the gadget-local copy $x^{(j)}_{v,c}$ remains unconstrained with respect to $x_{v,c}$. This assignment preserves the non-bounding property of gadget 2-cycles: equality clauses introduced by owners are 2-CNF and contractible, and they do not create 3-chains filling gadget-local 2-cycles. Consequently the homology lower bounds in Section~13 remain valid under the ownership scheme.

label: lem:Delta-bound
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_tex:
\label{lem:Delta-bound}
Fix \(\alpha>0\) and let \(k=\gamma n\) satisfy \(\Phi(\gamma;\alpha)>\eta>0\). Then there exists constants \(c=c(\eta)>0\) and \(n_0\) such that for all \(n\ge n_0\),
\[
\Delta \le \exp(-c n)\;(\mathbb{E}X_k)^2.
\]
Consequently \(X_k=(1+o(1))\mathbb{E}X_k\) with probability \(1-\exp(-\Theta(n))\).
statement_text: Fix \(α>0\) and let \(k=γ n\) satisfy \(Φ(γ;α)>η>0\). Then there exists constants \(c=c(η)>0\) and \(n_0\) such that for all \(n ≥ n_0\), \[ Δ ≤ exp (-c n) ( E X_k)^2. \] Consequently \(X_k=(1+o(1)) E X_k\) with probability \(1-exp (-Θ(n))\).
title: Pair-counting bound for \(Δ\)

label: lem:chen-stein
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_tex:
\label{lem:chen-stein}
Fix an integer \(R\ge 1\). Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be any collection of candidate \(k\)-cubes such that the Hamming distance between any two cubes in \(\mathcal{A}\) is at least \(R\) (so that any clause can touch at most \(D(R)\) cubes, with \(D(R)\) independent of \(n\)). Then for \(n\to\infty\),
\[
d_{TV}\!\Big(\mathcal{L}\big((I_u)_{u\in\mathcal{A}}\big),\bigotimes_{u\in\mathcal{A}}\mathrm{Bernoulli}\big(p_u\big)\Big) \le \varepsilon_n,
\]
where \(p_u=(1-q_{k,n})^m\) and \(\varepsilon_n\to 0\) (the rate depends on \(R\), \(\alpha\) and \(\gamma\) but not on \(|\mathcal{A}|\) as long as \(|\mathcal{A}|\) is fixed).

Let \( A \) be any collection of candidate \(k\)-cubes such that the Hamming distance between any two cubes in \( A \) is at least \(R\) (so that any clause can touch at most \(D(R)\) cubes, with \(D(R)\) independent of \(n\)). Then for \(n → ∞ \), \[ d_ TV ( L ((I_u)_ u ∈ A ), otimes_ u ∈ A Bernoulli (p_u ) ) ≤ ε_n, \] where \(p_u=(1-q_ k,n )^m\) and \(ε_n → 0\) (the rate depends on \(R\), \(α\) and \(γ\) but not on \(| A |\) as long as \(| A |\) is fixed).

label: thm:random-betti
paper_title: An Intrinsic Barrier for Resolving P = NP (2-SAT as Flat, 3-SAT as High-Dimensional Void-Rich)
statement_tex:
\label{thm:random-betti}
Fix \(\alpha>0\) and let \(k=k(n)=\gamma n\) with \(\gamma\in(0,1)\). Suppose
\[
\Phi(\gamma;\alpha)=H(\gamma)+(1-\gamma)\ln 2 - \alpha q(\gamma) > 0,
\]
with \(q(\gamma)\) as in \eqref{eq:q-limit}. Then there exists \(c(\gamma,\alpha)>0\) such that for random 3-CNF \(F\) with \(m=\alpha n\) clauses,
\[
\Pr\big[\beta_k(S(F)) \ge \exp(c n)\big] \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} 1.
\]
In the complementary regime \(\Phi(\gamma;\alpha)<0\) we have \(\mathbb{E}X_k=o(1)\) and hence w.h.p.\ no \(k\)-cubes survive.
statement_text: Fix \(α>0\) and let \(k=k(n)=γ n\) with \(γ ∈ (0,1)\). Suppose \[ Φ(γ;α)=H(γ)+(1-γ)ln 2 - α q(γ) > 0, \] with \(q(γ)\) as in . Then there exists \(c(γ,α)>0\) such that for random 3-CNF \(F\) with \(m=α n\) clauses, \[ Pr [β_k(S(F)) ≥ exp (c n) ] xrightarrow [n → ∞ ] 1. \] In the complementary regime \(Φ(γ;α)<0\) we have \( E X_k=o(1)\) and hence w.h.p.\ no \(k\)-cubes survive.

label: def:fingerprint_intro
paper_title: Symmetric Parameterised Holants on Hypergraphs: Towards a Classification for Parameterised VCSPs
statement_tex:
\label{def:fingerprint_intro}
Let $a$ be a positive integer and let $s$ be a signature. If $s(0)\neq 0$ then the \emph{fingerprint} of $a$ and $s$ is defined as
    \[\chi(a,s) := \sum_{\sigma} (-1)^{|\sigma|-1} (|\sigma|-1)! \cdot \prod_{B \in \sigma} \frac{s(|B|)}{s(0)} \,,\]
    where the sum is over all partitions $\sigma$ of $[a]$ and $|\sigma|$ denotes the number of blocks $B \in \sigma$. For technical reasons, if $s(x)=0$ for all $x$, we set $\chi(a,s)=0$. In all remaining cases, i.e., $s(0)=0$ but $s(x)\neq 0$ for some $x>0$, the fingerprint is undefined and we set $\chi(a,s)=\bot$.
statement_text: Let a be a positive integer and let s be a signature. If s(0) ≠ 0 then the fingerprint of a and s is defined as \[χ(a,s) := Σ _ σ (-1)^ |σ|-1 (|σ|-1)! · Π _ B ∈ σ frac s(|B|) s(0) ,\] where the sum is over all partitions σ of [a] and |σ| denotes the number of blocks B ∈ σ . For technical reasons, if s(x)=0 for all x , we set χ(a,s)=0 . In all remaining cases, i.e., s(0)=0 but s(x) ≠ 0 for some x>0 , the fingerprint is undefined and we set χ(a,s)=bot .
title: Signature Fingerprints

label: def:sigtype_intro
paper_title: Symmetric Parameterised Holants on Hypergraphs: Towards a Classification for Parameterised VCSPs
statement_text: Let S be a finite set of signatures. We say that S is of type T [1] if χ(a,s)=0 for all s ∈ S , a ≥ 2 , T [2] if χ(a,s)=0 for all s ∈ S , a ≥ 3 , but there exists s ∈ S with χ(2,s) ≠ 0 , and T [ ∞ ] otherwise, i.e., there exists s ∈ S and a ≥ 3 such that χ(a,s) ≠ 0 .
title: Types of Signature Sets

label: def:mobius

statement_tex:
\label{def:mobius}
    Let $S$ be a finite set and let $\rho=\{B_1,\dots,B_t\}$ be a partition of $S$. Let furthermore $\sigma$ be a partition of $S$ with $\sigma \leq \rho$. For each $i\in [t]$, let $\sigma^i$ be the subpartition of $\sigma$ refining $\{B_i\}$, that is, $\sigma = \dot{\cup}_{i=1}^t \sigma^i$ and $\sigma^i$ is a partition of $B_i$ for all $i\in [t]$. Then the \emph{M\"obius function} of $\sigma$ and $\rho$ is defined as follows:
    \[ \mu_S(\sigma,\rho):=  \prod_{i=1}^t (-1)^{|\sigma^i|-1}(|\sigma^i|-1)! \,,\]
    where $0!=1$ as usual. We will drop the subscript $S$ of $\mu_S$ if it is clear from the context and we will further simplify notation by writing $\mu(\rho)$ instead of $\mu(\bot, \rho)$.

Then the M\"obius function of σ and ρ is defined as follows: \[ μ_S(σ,ρ):= Π _ i=1 ^t (-1)^ |σ^i|-1 (|σ^i|-1)! ,\] where 0!=1 as usual. We will drop the subscript S of μ_S if it is clear from the context and we will further simplify notation by writing μ(ρ) instead of μ(bot , ρ) .

statement_tex:
Let $(P, \kappa), (P', \kappa')$ be two parameterised counting problems. An \emph{FPT Turing-reduction} from $(P, \kappa)$ to $(P', \kappa')$ is an algorithm $\mathbb{A}$ to compute $P(x)$ that has oracle access to $(P', \kappa')$ satisfying the following:

\begin{itemize}
\item There is a computable function $f$ such that $\mathbb{A}$ computes $P(x)$ in time $f(\kappa(x))\cdot |x|^{O(1)}$.
\item There is a computable function $g$ such that for any queried instance $y$, we have $\kappa'(y) \leq g(\kappa(x))$.
\end{itemize}

If in particular, $\mathbb{A}$ computes $P(x)$ in time $f(\kappa(x))\cdot O(|x|)$ making at most $f(\kappa(x))$ queries to the oracle, then we call $\mathbb{A}$ a \emph{linear FPT Turing-reduction}.

We write $(P, \kappa) \leq^{\mathsf{FPT}}_{\mathsf{T}} (P', \kappa')$ $($resp. $(P, \kappa) \fptlinred (P', \kappa'))$ if there is an FPT Turing-reduction $($resp. linear FPT Turing-reduction$)$ from $(P, \kappa)$ to $(P', \kappa')$.
statement_text: Let (P, κ), (P', κ') be two parameterised counting problems. An FPT Turing-reduction from (P, κ) to (P', κ') is an algorithm A to compute P(x) that has oracle access to (P', κ') satisfying the following: There is a computable function f such that A computes P(x) in time f(κ(x)) · |x|^ O(1) . There is a computable function g such that for any queried instance y , we have κ'(y) ≤ g(κ(x)) . If in particular, A computes P(x) in time f(κ(x)) · O(|x|) making at most f(κ(x)) queries to the oracle, then we call A a linear FPT Turing-reduction . We write (P, κ) ≤ ^ FPT _ T (P', κ') ( resp. (P, κ) ≤ ^ FPT-lin _ T (P', κ')) if there is an FPT Turing-reduction ( resp. linear FPT Turing-reduction ) from (P, κ) to (P', κ') .
title: Parameterised Reductions

Then there is a computable function $g$ such that $(P,\kappa)$ can be solved in time $g(\kappa(x))\cdot O(\log^d(|x|)\cdot |x|^c)$.

A \emph{group action} of $G$ on $X$ is a function $\alpha: G \times X \rightarrow X$, denoted by $\alpha(g,x) = g \cdot x$, that satisfies the following properties: $e \cdot x = x$ for all $x\in X$, where $e\in G$ is the identity element of $G$, and $g \cdot(h \cdot x)=(gh) \cdot x$ for all $g,h\in G$ and $x\in X$.

paper_title: On the Bit Size of Sum-of-Squares Proofs for Symmetric Formulations
statement_tex:
Let a group $G$ act on a set $X$.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item For $x \in X$, the set $Orb_x = \{g \cdot x \in X \ | \ g \in G \}$ is called the \emph{$G$-orbit} of $x$.
        \item For $x \in X$, the set $Stab_x = \{ g \in G \ | \ g \cdot x = x \}$ is called the \emph{stabilizer} of $x$ in $G$.
        \item The set of all distinct $G$-orbits of $X$ is called the \emph{quotient set} of $X$ by $G$, denoted $X/G$.
        \item An element $x \in X$ is a \emph{fixed point} if its $G$-orbit consists only of $x$, i.e., $Orb_x = \{x\}$. Equivalently, $x$ is a fixed point if its stabilizer is the entire group $G$, i.e., $Stab_x = G$.
    \end{itemize}

An element x ∈ X is a fixed point if its G -orbit consists only of x , i.e., Orb_x = {x} . Equivalently, x is a fixed point if its stabilizer is the entire group G , i.e., Stab_x = G .

statement_text: Let G be a finite group that can act on the indices 1, ... , n (e.g., a subgroup of S_n ). For g ∈ G and a multi-index α = (α_1, ... , α_n) ∈ N ^n , we define the action of g on α as g · α = (α_ g^ -1 (1) , ... , α_ g^ -1 (n) ) . For a monomial m = x^ α , the action of G on m is defined for any g ∈ G as: g · m := x^ g · α = x_1^ α_ g^ -1 (1) ... x_n^ α_ g^ -1 (n) = x_ g(1) ^ α_1 ... x_ g(n) ^ α_n . This action extends linearly to the set of polynomials R [x_1, ... , x_n] . Thus, for a polynomial p(x) = Σ _ i=0 ^m a_i x^ α_i , the action of g ∈ G on p is defined as g · p = Σ _ i=0 ^m a_i (g · x^ α_i ) . A polynomial p is said to be G -invariant if g · p = p for all g ∈ G . If G=S_n , where S_n is the symmetric group on n elements, the polynomial is called symmetric .

statement_tex: A program $P$ running in time $t(n)$ is \texttt{L}-consistent if $P(x)\in\{0,1,\bot\}$, $\forall x$, and if $P(x)\neq \bot$ then $P(x)=\chi_\texttt{L}(x)$.

paper_title: Formal Framework for Quantum Advantage
statement_tex: A program $P_U$ is quantum $\epsilon$-\texttt{L}-consistent if it generates a circuit $U$ that uses a dedicated qubit $q_0$ to signal its confidence. If the outcome of $q_0$ indicates "I know", ie $p(q_0=1)>1/2+\epsilon$, then a second qubit $q_1$ must yield the correct answer with high probability, ie $p(q_1=\chi_\texttt{L}(x))>1/2+\epsilon$. If $q_0$ indicates "I don't know", ie $p(q_0=0)>1/2+\epsilon$, the outcome of $q_1$ is disregarded.

statement_tex:
A Markov process $M = (\Omega,P)$ is defined by:
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item A finite state space $\Omega$.\footnote{In this work, we will always assume that $\Omega$ is finite. There is also a vast literature on Markov chains that considers infinite state spaces, or even continuous ones, but this is beyond the scope of our work.}
            \item A probability transition matrix $P \in \R_{\geq0}^{\Omega \times \Omega}$, such that every row sums to $1$.
        \end{enumerate}
        If we take a random variable $X_0$ according to some probability distribution on $\Omega$, and then select a sequence of random variables $X_1, X_2, \dots$ such that for all $t \in \N$ and $\omega_1,\omega_2 \in \Omega$,
        \[\P[X_t = \omega_2 | X_{t-1} = \omega_1] = P_{\omega_1,\omega_2},\]
        then we say that $X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots$ is a Markov chain. We say that the Markov chain transition from state $\omega_1 \in \Omega$ into state $\omega_2 \in \Omega$ with probability $P_{\omega_1,\omega_2}$.
statement_text: A Markov process M = (Ω,P) is defined by: A finite state space Ω . A probability transition matrix P ∈ R _ ≥ 0 ^ Ω × Ω , such that every row sums to 1 . If we take a random variable X_0 according to some probability distribution on Ω , and then select a sequence of random variables X_1, X_2, ... such that for all t ∈ N and ω_1,ω_2 ∈ Ω , \[ P [X_t = ω_2 | X_ t-1 = ω_1] = P_ ω_1,ω_2 ,\] then we say that X_0, X_1, X_2, ... is a Markov chain. We say that the Markov chain transition from state ω_1 ∈ Ω into state ω_2 ∈ Ω with probability P_ ω_1,ω_2 .

statement_tex:
Let $M = (\Omega,P)$ be a Markov process.
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item A distribution $\pi \in \Delta_{\Omega}$ is a \textit{stationary distribution} for $M$ if $\pi = \pi P$.
            \item A Markov chain is \textit{irreducible} if it is possible to reach any state from any other state through a sequence of transitions with non-zero probability. In other words, for all $\omega_1, \omega_2 \in \Omega$, there exists a $t \in \N$ such that $(P^t)_{\omega_1,\omega_2} > 0$.
        \end{enumerate}

statement_tex:
Let $M = (\Omega,P)$ be a Markov process with stationary distribution $\pi$. We say that $M$ is reversible with stationary distribution $\pi$ if for all $\omega_1,\omega_2 \in \Omega$, we have
        \[\pi_{\omega_1}P_{\omega_1,\omega_2} = \pi_{\omega_2}P_{\omega_2,\omega_1}.\]
        This condition is referred to as the detailed balance condition. If $M$ is irreducible, then $\pi$ is unique by \cref{thm:pi-unique} and so we simply say that $M$ is reversible.

If M is irreducible, then π is unique by cref thm:pi-unique and so we simply say that M is reversible.

statement_tex:
Let $G = (V,E)$ be an undirected graph with resistances $r : E \to \R_{>0}$, and let $M = (V,P)$ be the random walk on $G$ with resistances $r$.
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]

label: def:effective-resistance
paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{def:effective-resistance}
        Let $G = (V,E)$ be an undirected graph, with resistances $r : E \to \R_{>0}$.
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item A flow is a function $f : E \to \R$. We embed all flows in the flow space $\C^E = \Span\{\ket{e} : e \in E\}$ by
            \[\ket{f} = \sum_{e \in E} f_e\sqrt{r_e}\ket{e}.\]
            We refer to $\norm{\ket{f}}^2$ as the energy dissipated by $f$, or simply the energy of $f$.
            \item For any flow $f$, we define the net-flow $\delta_f : V \to \R$ as
            \[\delta_f(v) = \sum_{e \in N_-(v)} f_e - \sum_{e \in N_+(v)} f_e.\]
            If $\delta_f \equiv 0$, then $f$ is a circulation, and we define the circulation space as $\mathcal{C} = \{\ket{f} : f \text{ is a circulation}\}$.
            \item For any net-flow $\delta : V \to \R$, the set of corresponding flows $f$ such that $\delta_f = \delta$ forms an affine subspace, i.e., $\ket{f_\delta^{\min}} + \mathcal{C}$. We refer to $f_{\delta}^{\min}$ as the minimum-energy flow with net-flow $\delta$, and we write
            \[R(G,r;\delta) = \norm{\ket{f_{\delta}^{\min}}}^2.\]
            We refer to this as the effective resistance of net-flow $\delta$ in $G$ with resistances $r$.
        \end{enumerate}
statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be an undirected graph, with resistances r : E → R _ >0 . A flow is a function f : E → R . We embed all flows in the flow space C ^E = Span { |e rangle : e ∈ E} by \[ |f rangle = Σ _ e ∈ E f_e sqrt r_e |e rangle .\] We refer to | |f rangle | ^2 as the energy dissipated by f , or simply the energy of f . For any flow f , we define the net-flow δ_f : V → R as \[δ_f(v) = Σ _ e ∈ N_-(v) f_e - Σ _ e ∈ N_+(v) f_e.\] If δ_f equiv 0 , then f is a circulation, and we define the circulation space as C = { |f rangle : f is a circulation } . For any net-flow δ : V → R , the set of corresponding flows f such that δ_f = δ forms an affine subspace, i.e., |f_δ^ min rangle + C . We refer to f_ δ ^ min as the minimum-energy flow with net-flow δ , and we write \[R(G,r;δ) = | |f_ δ ^ min rangle | ^2.\] We refer to this as the effective resistance of net-flow δ in G with resistances r .

statement_tex:

statement_tex:
Let $\D$ be some finite domain, and for all $x \in \D$, we define $\ket{\sigma_x} \in \V$, $\ket{\tau_x} \in \V$ and $O_x \in \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M})$. Then, $P = \{(\ket{\sigma_x},\ket{\tau_x},O_x)\}_{x \in \D}$ is a state-conversion problem, and its adversary bound is the following optimization program:
        \begin{align*}
            \min\quad & \max_{x \in \D} \norm{\ket{w_x}}^2, \\
            \text{s.t.}\quad & \braket{\sigma_x}{\sigma_y} - \braket{\tau_x}{\tau_y} = \bra{w_x}\left(\left(I_{\mathcal{M}} - O_x^{\dagger}O_y\right) \otimes I_{\mathcal{W}}\right)\ket{w_y}, & \forall (x,y) \in \D, \\
            & \ket{w_x} \in \mathcal{M} \otimes \mathcal{W}, \text{ where } \mathcal{W} \text{ is a Hilbert space}, & \forall x \in \D.
        \end{align*}
        We denote the optimal value by $\ADV(P)$. If all the states satisfy $\norm{\ket{\sigma_x}} = \norm{\ket{\tau_x}} = 1$, for all $x \in \D$, then we say that this is a unit-norm state-conversion problem, and if the operations $O_x$ are unitaries, we say that $P$ is a unitary-oracle state-conversion problem. For a function $f : \Sigma_1 \to \Sigma_2$, we define $\ket{\sigma_x} = \ket{\perp}$ and $\ket{\tau_x} = \ket{f(x)}$, for all $x \in \D$, and we abbreviate the optimal value to $\ADV(\{(\ket{\bot}, \ket{f(x)}, O_x)\}_{x \in \D}) = \ADV(f, \{O_x\}_{x \in \D})$.

paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_tex:
Let $M = (V,P)$ be an irreducible, reversible Markov process, and let $G = (V,E)$ be the corresponding undirected graph with resistance function $r$, as in \cref{thm:random-walk-characterization}. For any net-flow $\delta \in \R^V$, we write $R_{\mathrm{eff}}(P;\delta) = R_{\mathrm{eff}}(G,r;\delta)$. We also write
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item For all $v,w \in V$, we write $R_{\mathrm{eff}}(G,r;v \leftrightarrow w) = R_{\mathrm{eff}}(G,r;\mathbbm{1}_v - \mathbbm{1}_w)$, i.e., the effective resistance between vertices $v$ and $w$.
            \item For any two distributions $\mu,\nu \in \Delta_V$, we write $R_{\mathrm{eff}}(G,r;\mu \leftrightarrow \nu) = R_{\mathrm{eff}}(G,r;\mu - \nu)$.
            \item For a distribution $\mu \in \Delta_V$ and a set $M \subseteq V$, we write
            \[R_{\mathrm{eff}}(G,r;\mu \leftrightarrow M) = \min_{\nu \in \Delta_V : \nu|_{V \setminus M} \equiv 0} R_{\mathrm{eff}}(G,r;\mu \leftrightarrow \nu).\]
        \end{enumerate}
        We extend all these notations $R(G,r;\cdot)$ to $R(P;\cdot)$ as well.
statement_text: Let M = (V,P) be an irreducible, reversible Markov process, and let G = (V,E) be the corresponding undirected graph with resistance function r , as in cref thm:random-walk-characterization . For any net-flow δ ∈ R ^V , we write R_ eff (P;δ) = R_ eff (G,r;δ) . We also write For all v,w ∈ V , we write R_ eff (G,r;v ↔ w) = R_ eff (G,r;m 1 _v - m 1 _w) , i.e., the effective resistance between vertices v and w . For any two distributions μ,ν ∈ Δ_V , we write R_ eff (G,r;μ ↔ ν) = R_ eff (G,r;μ - ν) . For a distribution μ ∈ Δ_V and a set M ⊆ V , we write \[R_ eff (G,r;μ ↔ M) = min _ ν ∈ Δ_V : ν|_ V \ M equiv 0 R_ eff (G,r;μ ↔ ν).\] We extend all these notations R(G,r; · ) to R(P; · ) as well.

\label{def:state-reflection-problem}
        Let $\D$ be a finite set. For all $x \in \D$, let $\ket{\sigma_x^+}, \ket{\sigma_x^-}$ be two orthogonal vectors in $\V$, and let $O_x$ be an operation on $\H$, such that $O_x^2 = I$. We refer to $\ket{w_x^+}$ and $\ket{w_x^-}$ as the positive and negative witnesses for $x$, and similarly to $\norm{\ket{w_x^+}}^2$ and $\norm{\ket{w_x^-}}^2$ as the positive and negative witness sizes for $x \in \D$, which write as $\mathsf{R}^+_x(w)$ and $\mathsf{R}^-_x(w)$.

statement_tex:
\label{thm:reformulation-state-conversion}
        Let $P = \{(\ket{\sigma_x}, \ket{\tau_x}, O_x)\}_{x \in \D}$ be a unit-norm unitary-oracle state-conversion problem, with input and output and oracle spaces $\V_1$, $\V_2$ and $\H$, respectively. For all $x \in \D$, we write
        \[\ket{\sigma_x^{\pm}} = \frac{\ket{\sigma_x} \oplus \pm\ket{\tau_x}}{\sqrt{2}} \in \V_1 \oplus \V_2, \qquad \text{and} \qquad \overline{O_x} = (X \otimes I)(O_x \oplus O_x^{\dagger}) \in \mathcal{L}(\H \oplus \H),\]
        where $X \otimes I$ acting on $\H \oplus \H$ swaps both copies of $\H$. Then, $R = \{(\ket{\sigma_x^+}, \ket{\sigma_x^-}, \overline{O_x})\}_{x \in \D}$ is a state-reflection problem, $\ADV(P) = \ADV(R)$, and there exists an optimal solution $\{\ket{w_x^{\pm}}\}_{x \in \D}$ to $R$ such that $\overline{O_x}\ket{w_x^{\pm}} = \pm\ket{w_x^{\pm}}$.

label: thm:las-vegas-algorithm
paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:las-vegas-algorithm}
        Let $\A$ be a quantum Monte-Carlo algorithm that implements the state-conversion problem given by $P = \{(\ket{\sigma_x}, \ket{\tau_x}, O_x)\}_{x \in \D}$, with run-time given by the random variable $T_x$, for every $x \in \D$. Then, for any choice of $(\alpha_t)_{t \in \N_0} \subseteq \R_{>0}$, we can implement a feasible solution $W := \{\ket{w_x^{\pm}}\}_{x \in \D}$ to the corresponding state-reflection problem $R := \{(\ket{\sigma_x} \pm \ket{\tau_x}, \pm(\ket{\sigma_x} \pm \ket{\tau_x}), \overline{O_x})\}_{x \in \D}$, with complexities
        \[\mathsf{W}_x^+ = \E\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T_x-1} \alpha_t\right], \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathsf{W}_x^- = \E\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T_x-1} \frac{1}{\alpha_t}\right].\]
        In particular, by choosing $\alpha_t = 1$, for all $t \in \N_0$, we obtain $\mathsf{W}_x^{\pm} = \E[T_x]$, and by choosing $\alpha_t = t+1$, we obtain $\mathsf{W}_x^+ = \E[T_x(T_x+1)/2] \in O(\E[T_x^2])$, and $\mathsf{W}_x^- \in O(1 + \E[\log(T_x)])$.

Then, for any choice of (α_t)_ t ∈ N _0 ⊆ R _ >0 , we can implement a feasible solution W := { |w_x^ pm rangle }_ x ∈ D to the corresponding state-reflection problem R := {( |σ_x rangle pm |τ_x rangle , pm ( |σ_x rangle pm |τ_x rangle ), overline O_x )}_ x ∈ D , with complexities \[ W _x^+ = E [ Σ _ t=0 ^ T_x-1 α_t ], qquad and qquad W _x^- = E [ Σ _ t=0 ^ T_x-1 frac 1 α_t ].\] In particular, by choosing α_t = 1 , for all t ∈ N _0 , we obtain W _x^ pm = E [T_x] , and by choosing α_t = t+1 , we obtain W _x^+ = E [T_x(T_x+1)/2] ∈ O( E [T_x^2]) , and W _x^- ∈ O(1 + E [ log (T_x)]) .

statement_tex:
\label{def:hyperedge-problem}
        Let $V$ be a finite set, and $R = \{(\ket{\sigma_x^{\pm}}, \pm\ket{\sigma_x^{\pm}}, O_x)\}_{x \in \D}$ be a state-reflection problem over $\mathcal{V} = \C^V$. Suppose in addition that we can write for all $x \in \D$,
        \[\ket{\sigma_x^+} := \delta_x \in \C^V, \qquad \text{and} \qquad \ket{\sigma_x^-} = U_x \in \C^V,\]
        such that
        \[U_x \text{ is constant on } \supp(\delta_x), \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_{v \in V} (\delta_x)_v = 0.\]
        Then, we say that $R$ is a hyperedge problem denoted by $\{(\delta_x,U_x,O_x)\}_{x \in \D}$, and we say that it implements the net-flow $\delta_x$ and the potential function $U_x$ through the hyperedge with vertices $V$.

Suppose in addition that we can write for all x ∈ D , \[ |σ_x^+ rangle := δ_x ∈ C ^V, qquad and qquad |σ_x^- rangle = U_x ∈ C ^V,\] such that \[U_x is constant on supp (δ_x), qquad and qquad Σ _ v ∈ V (δ_x)_v = 0.\] Then, we say that R is a hyperedge problem denoted by {(δ_x,U_x,O_x)}_ x ∈ D , and we say that it implements the net-flow δ_x and the potential function U_x through the hyperedge with vertices V .

label: thm:hyperedge-from-span-program
paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:hyperedge-from-span-program}
        Let $f : \D \to \{0,1\}$. For all $x \in \D$, we define net-flow $\delta_x$ and potential function $U_x$ on $\{s,t\}$, as
        \[\delta_x = \begin{cases}
            \mathbbm{1}_s - \mathbbm{1}_t, & \text{if } f(x) = 1, \\
            0, & f(x) = 0,
        \end{cases} \qquad \text{and} \qquad U_x = \begin{cases}
            0, & \text{if } f(x) = 1, \\
            -\mathbbm{1}_t, & f(x) = 0.
        \end{cases}\]

        On the one hand, let $\mathcal{P} = (\H, x \mapsto \H(x), \K, \ket{w_0})$ be a span program on $\D$ that computes $f$. Let $\{\ket{w_x}\}_{x \in \D}$ be a set of witnesses for $\mathcal{P}$. We write
        \[\ket{w_x^+} = \begin{cases}
            \ket{w_x}, & \text{if } f(x) = 1, \\
            0, & \text{if } f(x) = 0,
        \end{cases} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \ket{w_x^-} = \begin{cases}
            0, & \text{if } f(x) = 1, \\
            \ket{w_x}, & \text{if } f(x) = 0.
        \end{cases}\]
        Then, $\{\ket{w_x^{\pm}}\}_{x \in \D}$ is a feasible solution for the hyperedge problem $R = \{(\delta_x, U_x, 2\Pi_{\H(x)} - I)\}_{x \in \D}$.

        Conversely, let $\{\ket{w_x^{\pm}}\}_{x \in \D}$ be a feasible solution to the hyperedge problem $R = \{(\delta_x, U_x, O_x)\}_{x \in \D}$, where the oracles $O_x$ act on $\H$. We let $\H(x)$ be the $+1$-eigenspace of $O_x$. Then, there exists a span program $\mathcal{P} = (\H, x \mapsto \H(x), \K, \ket{w_0})$ that computes $f$, with
        \[C(\mathcal{P})^2 \leq \max\left\{\max_{x \in f^{-1}(1)} \norm{\ket{w_x^+}}^2, \max_{x \in f^{-1}(0)} \norm{\ket{w_x^-}}^2\right\}.\]
statement_text: Let f : D → {0,1} . For all x ∈ D , we define net-flow δ_x and potential function U_x on {s,t} , as \[δ_x = m 1 _s - m 1 _t, & if f(x) = 1, 0, & f(x) = 0, qquad and qquad U_x = 0, & if f(x) = 1, -m 1 _t, & f(x) = 0. \] On the one hand, let P = ( H , x mapsto H (x), K , |w_0 rangle ) be a span program on D that computes f . Let { |w_x rangle }_ x ∈ D be a set of witnesses for P . We write \[ |w_x^+ rangle = |w_x rangle , & if f(x) = 1, 0, & if f(x) = 0, qquad and qquad |w_x^- rangle = 0, & if f(x) = 1, |w_x rangle , & if f(x) = 0. \] Then, { |w_x^ pm rangle }_ x ∈ D is a feasible solution for the hyperedge problem R = {(δ_x, U_x, 2Π_ H (x) - I)}_ x ∈ D . Conversely, let { |w_x^ pm rangle }_ x ∈ D be a feasible solution to the hyperedge problem R = {(δ_x, U_x, O_x)}_ x ∈ D , where the oracles O_x act on H . We let H (x) be the +1 -eigenspace of O_x . Then, there exists a span program P = ( H , x mapsto H (x), K , |w_0 rangle ) that computes f , with \[C( P )^2 ≤ max {max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (1) | |w_x^+ rangle | ^2, max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (0) | |w_x^- rangle | ^2 }.\]
title: Hyperedge from a span program

label: thm:known-marked-fraction-recovery
paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:known-marked-fraction-recovery}
        Let $V$ be a finite set, and let $\pi \in \Delta_V$. For all $x \in \D$ in a finite domain $\D$, let $M_x \subseteq V$, such that $\P_{v \sim \pi}[v \in M_x] = \varepsilon$, for some fixed $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. We write
        \[\ket{\psi_x} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}\sum_{v \in M_x}\sqrt{\pi_v}\ket{v},\]
        and we define the state-reflection problems $R = \{(\ket{\perp} + \ket{\psi_x}, \ket{\perp} - \ket{\psi_x}, O_x)\}_{x \in \D}$ and $R' = \{(\mathbbm{1}_{\perp} - \frac{\pi|_{M_x}}{\varepsilon}, \mathbbm{1}_{\perp} + \mathbbm{1}_{M_x}, O_x)\}_{x \in \D}$. Then, the feasible regions for $R$ and $R'$ are identical, and $R'$ is a hyperedge problem.
statement_text: Let V be a finite set, and let π ∈ Δ_V . For all x ∈ D in a finite domain D , let M_x ⊆ V , such that P _ v π [v ∈ M_x] = ε , for some fixed ε ∈ (0,1) . We write \[ |ψ_x rangle = frac 1 sqrt ε Σ _ v ∈ M_x sqrt π_v |v rangle ,\] and we define the state-reflection problems R = {( |perp rangle + |ψ_x rangle , |perp rangle - |ψ_x rangle , O_x)}_ x ∈ D and R' = {(m 1 _ perp - frac π|_ M_x ε , m 1 _ perp + m 1 _ M_x , O_x)}_ x ∈ D . Then, the feasible regions for R and R' are identical, and R' is a hyperedge problem.

label: def:generalized-graph-composition
paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{def:generalized-graph-composition}
        Let $G = (V,E)$ be a hypergraph, with boundary vertices $B \subseteq V$, and let $\D$ be a finite domain. For every hyperedge $e \in E$, let $R^e = \{(\delta_x^e, U_x^e, O_x^e)\}_{x \in \D}$ be a hyperedge problem. For all $v \in  V$ and $x \in \D$, we write $\delta_x(v) = \sum_{e \in N(v)} \delta_x^e(v)$. Suppose that
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item For all internal nodes $v \in V \setminus B$, the net-flow vanishes, i.e., $\delta_x(v) = 0$.
            \item The potential function is uniquely defined at every vertex $v \in V$, i.e., $U_x^e(v) = U_x(v)$, for all $e \in N(v)$.
        \end{enumerate}
        Then, we say that $(G,B,(R^e)_{e \in E})$ is an instance of the generalized graph composition framework, that implements the hyperedge problem $R = \{(\delta_x, U_x, \bigoplus_{e \in E} O_x^e)\}_{x \in \D}$ on vertex set $B$.
statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be a hypergraph, with boundary vertices B ⊆ V , and let D be a finite domain. For every hyperedge e ∈ E , let R^e = {(δ_x^e, U_x^e, O_x^e)}_ x ∈ D be a hyperedge problem. For all v ∈ V and x ∈ D , we write δ_x(v) = Σ _ e ∈ N(v) δ_x^e(v) . Suppose that For all internal nodes v ∈ V \ B , the net-flow vanishes, i.e., δ_x(v) = 0 . The potential function is uniquely defined at every vertex v ∈ V , i.e., U_x^e(v) = U_x(v) , for all e ∈ N(v) . Then, we say that (G,B,(R^e)_ e ∈ E ) is an instance of the generalized graph composition framework, that implements the hyperedge problem R = {(δ_x, U_x, oplus_ e ∈ E O_x^e)}_ x ∈ D on vertex set B .
title: Generalized graph composition

label: thm:generalized-graph-composition
paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:generalized-graph-composition}
        Let $(G = (V,E),B,(R^e)_{e \in E})$ be an instance of the generalized graph composition, implementing the hyperedge problem $R$. For all $e \in E$, suppose that $w^e = \{\ket{(w^e)_x^{\pm}}\}_{x \in \D}$ is a feasible solution to $R^e$. For all $x \in \D$, let
        \[\ket{w_x^{\pm}} := \bigoplus_{e \in E} \ket{(w^e)_x^{\pm}}.\]
        Then, $w = \{\ket{w_x^{\pm}}\}_{x \in \D}$ forms a feasible solution to $R$, with $\mathsf{R}_x^{\pm}(w) = \sum_{e \in E} \mathsf{R}_x^{\pm}(w^e)$, for all $x \in \D$.
statement_text: Let (G = (V,E),B,(R^e)_ e ∈ E ) be an instance of the generalized graph composition, implementing the hyperedge problem R . For all e ∈ E , suppose that w^e = { |(w^e)_x^ pm rangle }_ x ∈ D is a feasible solution to R^e . For all x ∈ D , let \[ |w_x^ pm rangle := oplus_ e ∈ E |(w^e)_x^ pm rangle .\] Then, w = { |w_x^ pm rangle }_ x ∈ D forms a feasible solution to R , with R _x^ pm (w) = Σ _ e ∈ E R _x^ pm (w^e) , for all x ∈ D .
title: Composition of hyperedges

label: thm:path-cut-theorem
paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:path-cut-theorem}
        Let $G = (V,E)$ be a hypergraph, with boundary vertices $B \subseteq V$ and hyperedge problems $R^e = \{(\delta_x^e, U_x^e, O_x^e)\}_{x \in \D}$ for all $e \in E$. Suppose that for every $x \in \D$ and $e \in E$, the total flow vector $\delta_x^e$ has support on at most two vertices, and $U_x^e = 1$ for those vertices, and $0$ everywhere else. Then, for every $x \in \D$, we can make a simple graph $G(x) = (V,E(x))$, where we include all the edges $uv$ that are connected by the unit flow in the hyperedge problem. Suppose that $G(x)$ connects exactly two boundary vertices $\{s_x,t_x\}$. Then, for all $x \in \D$, let $C_x \subseteq E$ be a cut that certifies that all the other boundary vertices cannot  be reached from $s_x$ or $t_x$. Then, we can generate an instance to generalized graph composition with witness complexities
        \[\mathsf{R}_x^+(w) = R_{\mathrm{eff}}(G(x), e \mapsto \mathsf{R}_x^+(w^e), s_x \leftrightarrow t_x), \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathsf{R}_x^-(w) = \sum_{e \in C_x} \mathsf{R}_x^-(w^e),\]
        where all $w^e$'s are feasible solutions to the $R^e$'s.
statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be a hypergraph, with boundary vertices B ⊆ V and hyperedge problems R^e = {(δ_x^e, U_x^e, O_x^e)}_ x ∈ D for all e ∈ E . Suppose that for every x ∈ D and e ∈ E , the total flow vector δ_x^e has support on at most two vertices, and U_x^e = 1 for those vertices, and 0 everywhere else. Then, for every x ∈ D , we can make a simple graph G(x) = (V,E(x)) , where we include all the edges uv that are connected by the unit flow in the hyperedge problem. Suppose that G(x) connects exactly two boundary vertices {s_x,t_x} . Then, for all x ∈ D , let C_x ⊆ E be a cut that certifies that all the other boundary vertices cannot be reached from s_x or t_x . Then, we can generate an instance to generalized graph composition with witness complexities \[ R _x^+(w) = R_ eff (G(x), e mapsto R _x^+(w^e), s_x ↔ t_x), qquad and qquad R _x^-(w) = Σ _ e ∈ C_x R _x^-(w^e),\] where all w^e 's are feasible solutions to the R^e 's.
title: Resistance-cut theorem for function evaluation and database update

paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_tex:
Let $x \in \{0,1\}^n \setminus \{0^n\}$, and let $i(x)$ be the first index containing a $1$, i.e., $i(x) = \min\{i \in [n] : x_i = 1\}$. The graph composition construction from \cref{fig:first-marked-index-finding} computes $i(x)$ with complexities

label: def:weighting-scheme
paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{def:weighting-scheme}
        Let $T = (V,E)$ be a decision tree with root node $r \in V$, and $w : V \to \R_{\geq0}$. We say that $w$ is a weighting scheme for $T$, if:
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item $w_v = 0$ for all leafs $v$.
            \item For any internal node $v$ with children $C_v \subseteq V$, we have matrices $0 \preceq X,Y \in \C^{C_v \times C_v}$ such that $X[c_1,c_2] - Y[c_1,c_2] = 1$, for all $c_1,c_2 \in C_V$ such that $c_1 \neq c_2$, and $w_v - w_c \geq X[c,c] + Y[c,c]$ for all $c \in C_v$.
        \end{enumerate}
        We say that $w_r$ is the weight of the tree, and we write
        \[\mathsf{WDT}(T) = \min_{w \text{ weighting scheme for } T} w_r.\]
statement_text: Let T = (V,E) be a decision tree with root node r ∈ V , and w : V → R _ ≥ 0 . We say that w is a weighting scheme for T , if: w_v = 0 for all leafs v . For any internal node v with children C_v ⊆ V , we have matrices 0 preceq X,Y ∈ C ^ C_v × C_v such that X[c_1,c_2] - Y[c_1,c_2] = 1 , for all c_1,c_2 ∈ C_V such that c_1 ≠ c_2 , and w_v - w_c ≥ X[c,c] + Y[c,c] for all c ∈ C_v . We say that w_r is the weight of the tree, and we write \[ WDT (T) = min _ w weighting scheme for T w_r.\]

paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_tex: Let $T = (V,E)$ be a decision tree with root node $r \in V$ and weighting scheme $w$, computing a function $f : \Sigma_I^n \supseteq \D \to \Sigma_O$. Then, we can compute $f$ with bounded error using $O(w_r)$ queries. Consequently, $\mathsf{Q}(f) \in O(\mathsf{WDT}(f))$.
statement_text: Let T = (V,E) be a decision tree with root node r ∈ V and weighting scheme w , computing a function f : Σ_I^n ⊇ D → Σ_O . Then, we can compute f with bounded error using O(w_r) queries. Consequently, Q (f) ∈ O( WDT (f)) .

label: thm:optimal-weight-assignment
paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_text: Let T = (V,E) be a decision tree with root node r ∈ V . Its optimal weighting scheme is computed by setting all the weight of all the leaf nodes to 0 , and then for every internal node v ∈ V with children C_v ⊆ V , recursively computing the semi-definite program w_v := min quad & max _ c ∈ C_v (w_c + X[c,c] + Y[c,c]) s.t. quad & X[c_1,c_2] - Y[c_1,c_2] = 1, & if c_1,c_2 ∈ C_v, c_1 ≠ c_2, & 0 preceq X,Y ∈ R ^ C_v × C_v .

statement_tex:
Let $G = (V,E)$ be a connected, undirected graph, with resistances $r : E \to \R_{>0}$, such that $\sum_{e \in E} r_e^{-1} = 1/2$. Let $\D$ be a finite domain, and for all $x \in \D$, let $M_x \subseteq V$. Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a set of database entries, and for all $v \in V$ and $x \in \D$, let $D_{v,x} \in \mathcal{S}$. Now, assume we have feasible solutions implementing the following operations:
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item For all $v \in V$, let $S_v$ be a hyperedge that computes $D_{v,x}$, for all $x \in \D$. We write the positive and negative witness sizes as $(\mathsf{S}_v)_x^{\pm}$.
            \item For all $vw = e \in E$, let $\mathsf{U}_e$ be a hyperedge that updates $D_{v,x}$ to $D_{w,x}$, for all $ \in \D$. We write the positive and negative witness sizes as $(\mathsf{U}_e)_x^{\pm}$.
            \item For all $v \in V$ and $D \in \mathcal{S}$, let $C_{v,D}$ be a span program that checks whether $v \in M_x$, for all $x \in \D$, whenever $D = D_{v,x}$. We write the positive and negative witness sizes as $(\mathsf{C}_{v,D})_x^{\pm}$.

label: thm:unified-quantum-walk-search
paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:unified-quantum-walk-search}
        Let $(G,r,x \mapsto M_x,(v,x) \mapsto D_{v,x}, \{S_v\}_{v \in V}, \{U_e\}_{e \in E}, \{C_{v,D}\}_{v \in V, D \in \mathcal{S}})$ be an instance of quantum walk search on $\D$, and let $\sigma \in \Delta_V$. We write
        \[\mathsf{S}^{\pm} := \max_{v \in D}\max_{x \in \D} (\mathsf{S}_v)_x^{\pm}, \qquad \mathsf{U}^{\pm} := \max_{e \in E} \max_{x \in \D} (\mathsf{U}_e)_x^{\pm}, \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathsf{C}^{\pm} := \max_{v \in V}\max_{x \in \D} (\mathsf{C}_{v,D_{v,x}})_x^{\pm},\]
        and we let $\mathsf{M} := \sqrt{\mathsf{M}^+\mathsf{M}^-}$, with $\mathsf{M} \in \{\mathsf{S}, \mathsf{U}, \mathsf{C}\}$. Let $t \geq 1$, and let $R \geq 0$ such that for all $x \in \D_+$, we have $R_{\mathrm{eff}}(P^t, \sigma \leftrightarrow M_x) \leq R$. Then, we can solve the detection version of the quantum walk search problem with a span program $\mathcal{P}$ with complexity
        \[C(\mathcal{P}) \in O\left(\mathsf{S} + \sqrt{tR}\mathsf{U} + \sqrt{1+R}\mathsf{C}\right).\]
statement_text: Let (G,r,x mapsto M_x,(v,x) mapsto D_ v,x , {S_v}_ v ∈ V , {U_e}_ e ∈ E , {C_ v,D }_ v ∈ V, D ∈ S ) be an instance of quantum walk search on D , and let σ ∈ Δ_V . We write \[ S ^ pm := max _ v ∈ D max _ x ∈ D ( S _v)_x^ pm , qquad U ^ pm := max _ e ∈ E max _ x ∈ D ( U _e)_x^ pm , qquad and qquad C ^ pm := max _ v ∈ V max _ x ∈ D ( C _ v,D_ v,x )_x^ pm ,\] and we let M := sqrt M ^+ M ^- , with M ∈ { S , U , C } . label: thm:var-time-quantum-walk-detection
paper_title: Quantum walks through generalized graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:var-time-quantum-walk-detection}
        Suppose we have the instance of quantum walk search $(G, r, x \mapsto M_x, (v,x) \mapsto D_{v,x}, \{S_v\}_{v \in V}, \{U_e\}_{e \in E}, \{C_{v,D}\}_{v \in V, D \in \mathcal{S}})$. Let $M = (V,P)$ be the corresponding random walk on $G$, with stationary distribution $\pi \in \Delta_V$. Let $\sigma,\tau \in \Delta_V$ be distributions with full support. We write, for all $v \in V$, $e \in E$ and $D \in \mathcal{S}$,
        \[\mathsf{S}_v^{\pm} := \max_{x \in \D_{\pm}} (\mathsf{S}_v)_x^{\pm}, \qquad \mathsf{U}_e^{\pm} := \max_{x \in \D_{\pm}} (\mathsf{U}_e)_x^{\pm}, \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathsf{C}_{v,D}^{\pm} := \max_{x \in \D_{\pm}} (\mathsf{C}_{v,D})_x^{\pm}.\]
        Next, we take two different definitions of several quantities:
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item Let $R := \max_{x \in \D_+} R_{\mathrm{eff}}(P; \sigma \leftrightarrow M_x)$, and for all $x \in \D_+$, let $\nu_x \in \Delta_{M_x}$ be the target distribution that minimizes the flow between $\sigma$ and $M_x$, i.e., $R_{\mathrm{eff}}(P; \sigma \leftrightarrow M_x) = R_{\mathrm{eff}}(P; \sigma - \nu_x)$. For all $x \in \D_+$, let $\varepsilon_x := \E_{v \sim \tau}[(\nu_x)_v^2/\tau_v]^{-1}$, and let $\varepsilon := \min_{x \in \D_+} \varepsilon_x$.
            \item For all $x \in \D_+$, let $\varepsilon_x = \P_{v \sim \tau} [v \in M_x]$, and $\nu_x := (\tau|_{M_x})/\varepsilon_x \in \Delta_{M_x}$. Next, let $\varepsilon = \min_{x \in \D_+} \varepsilon_x$, and $R := \max_{x \in \D_+} R_{\mathrm{eff}}(P; \mu_x - \nu_x)$.
        \end{enumerate}
        In both cases, we can solve the detection version of the quantum walk search problem with a span program $\mathcal{P}$, with complexities
        \begin{align*}
            w_+(x,\mathcal{P}) &\in O\left(\frac{\underset{v \sim \sigma}{\E}[(\mathsf{S}_v)_x^+]}{\underset{v \sim \sigma}{\E}[\mathsf{S}_v^+]} + \frac{R_{\mathrm{eff}}\left(G, r \circ \frac{(\mathsf{U}_{\cdot})_x^+}{\mathsf{U}_{\cdot}^+}; \sigma - \nu_x\right)}{R} + \underset{v \sim \tau}{\E} \left[\frac{(\nu_x)_v^2}{\tau_v} \cdot \frac{\varepsilon(\mathsf{C}_{v,D_{v,x}})_x^+}{\mathsf{C}_{v,D_{v,x}}^+}\right] \right) \subseteq O(1), \\
            w_-(x,\mathcal{P}) &\in O\left(\underset{v \sim \sigma}{\E}\left[\mathsf{S}_v^+\right] \cdot \underset{v \sim \sigma}{\E} \left[(\mathsf{S}_v)_x^-\right] + R \cdot \underset{\substack{v \sim \pi \\ w \sim P_{v\cdot}}}{\E} \left[\mathsf{U}^+_{vw}(\mathsf{U}_{vw})_x^-\right] + \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \cdot \underset{v \sim \tau}{\E} \left[\mathsf{C}_{v,D_{v,x}}^+(\mathsf{C}_{v,D_{v,x}})_x^-\right]\right),
        \end{align*}
        for $x \in \D_+$ and $x \in \D_-$, respectively.
statement_text: Suppose we have the instance of quantum walk search (G, r, x mapsto M_x, (v,x) mapsto D_ v,x , {S_v}_ v ∈ V , {U_e}_ e ∈ E , {C_ v,D }_ v ∈ V, D ∈ S ) . Let M = (V,P) be the corresponding random walk on G , with stationary distribution π ∈ Δ_V . Let σ,τ ∈ Δ_V be distributions with full support. We write, for all v ∈ V , e ∈ E and D ∈ S , \[ S _v^ pm := max _ x ∈ D _ pm ( S _v)_x^ pm , qquad U _e^ pm := max _ x ∈ D _ pm ( U _e)_x^ pm , qquad and qquad C _ v,D ^ pm := max _ x ∈ D _ pm ( C _ v,D )_x^ pm .\] Next, we take two different definitions of several quantities: Let R := max _ x ∈ D _+ R_ eff (P; σ ↔ M_x) , and for all x ∈ D _+ , let ν_x ∈ Δ_ M_x be the target distribution that minimizes the flow between σ and M_x , i.e., R_ eff (P; σ ↔ M_x) = R_ eff (P; σ - ν_x) . For all x ∈ D _+ , let ε_x := E _ v τ [(ν_x)_v^2/τ_v]^ -1 , and let ε := min _ x ∈ D _+ ε_x . For all x ∈ D _+ , let ε_x = P _ v τ [v ∈ M_x] , and ν_x := (τ|_ M_x )/ε_x ∈ Δ_ M_x . Next, let ε = min _ x ∈ D _+ ε_x , and R := max _ x ∈ D _+ R_ eff (P; μ_x - ν_x) . In both cases, we can solve the detection version of the quantum walk search problem with a span program P , with complexities w_+(x, P ) & ∈ O (frac underset v σ E [( S _v)_x^+] underset v σ E [ S _v^+] + frac R_ eff (G, r ∘ frac ( U _ · )_x^+ U _ · ^+ ; σ - ν_x ) R + underset v τ E [frac (ν_x)_v^2 τ_v · frac ε( C _ v,D_ v,x )_x^+ C _ v,D_ v,x ^+ ] ) ⊆ O(1), w_-(x, P ) & ∈ O (underset v σ E [ S _v^+ ] · underset v σ E [( S _v)_x^- ] + R · underset substack v π w P_ v · E [ U ^+_ vw ( U _ vw )_x^- ] + frac 1 ε · underset v τ E [ C _ v,D_ v,x ^+( C _ v,D_ v,x )_x^- ] ), for x ∈ D _+ and x ∈ D _- , respectively.

label: thm:feferman-vaught

statement_tex:
\label{thm:feferman-vaught}
Let $G_i,G_j$ be colored graphs, $T_i\subseteq V(G_i), T_j\subseteq V(G_j)$, $\bar u\in V(G_i)^h$, \\$\bar v\in V(G_i)^t$, $\bar w\in V(G_j)^\ell$ s.\ th.\ $V(G_i)\cap V(G_j)=\bar v$ and $T_i\cap V(G_i)\cap V(G_j)={T_j\cap V(G_i)\cap V(G_j)}$. 
Let $T=T_i\cup T_j$. 
Then for all $q\geq 0$, $tp_q(G_i\cup G_j,T,\bar u \bar v \bar w)$ is determined by $tp_q(G_i,T_i,\bar u \bar v)$ and $tp_q(G_j,T_j,\bar v \bar w)$.
Furthermore, there is an algorithm that computes $tp_q({G_i\cup G_j},T,\bar u \bar v \bar w)$ from $tp_q(G_i,T_i,\bar u \bar v)$ and $tp_q(G_j,T_j,\bar v \bar w)$ in time $f(q, t,h,\ell)$ for some computable function $f$.
statement_text: Let G_i,G_j be colored graphs, T_i ⊆ V(G_i), T_j ⊆ V(G_j) , bar u ∈ V(G_i)^h , bar v ∈ V(G_i)^t , bar w ∈ V(G_j)^ell s.\ th.\ V(G_i) ∩ V(G_j)=bar v and T_i ∩ V(G_i) ∩ V(G_j)= T_j ∩ V(G_i) ∩ V(G_j) . Let T=T_i ∪ T_j . Then for all q ≥ 0 , tp_q(G_i ∪ G_j,T,bar u bar v bar w) is determined by tp_q(G_i,T_i,bar u bar v) and tp_q(G_j,T_j,bar v bar w) . Furthermore, there is an algorithm that computes tp_q( G_i ∪ G_j ,T,bar u bar v bar w) from tp_q(G_i,T_i,bar u bar v) and tp_q(G_j,T_j,bar v bar w) in time f(q, t,h,ell ) for some computable function f .

paper_title: On Algorithmic Meta-Theorems for Solution Discovery: Tractability and Barriers
statement_tex:
Let $\phi(X)$ be an \MSO-formula with a free set variable~$X$, and let $q_s$ and $q_v$ be the numbers of set and vertex quantifiers in $\phi$, respectively. 

Let~$G$ be a graph with $\ell$ vertex-types $V_1,\ldots,V_\ell$, and define $q(\phi) = 2^{q_s} \cdot q_v$. 
Let $R \subseteq V(G)$ and let $\sigma_R(i) = |R \cap V_i|$. 

The \emph{shape} of $R$ is defined as follows:
\[
\overline{\sigma}_R(i) =
\begin{cases}
\bot & \text{if } q(\phi) \le \sigma_R(i) \le |V_i| - q(\phi), \\
\sigma_R(i) & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]

label: def:deg-size
paper_title: Semi-Algebraic Proof Systems for QBF
statement_text: The size of a Q - NS _ xspace xspace / Q - SA _ xspace xspace / Q - SOS _ xspace xspace refutation π ( size (π) ) is the number of monomials (counted with repetition) in q_p , q_u and q . The degree of π ( deg (π) ) is the maximum degree of any of the polynomials q_pp , q_u(1-2u) , and q . The Q-size of π ( qsize (π) ) is defined analogously to the size but accounts only for the monomials in the polynomials q_u . The existential Q-degree of π ( qdeg_ ∃ (π) ) is the maximum existential degree of any q_u , where the existential degree is the highest number of existentially quantified variables in any monomial.
